strengths: Identifies and clearly motivates a genuine gap in the typographic-attack literature: prior work and defenses focus almost exclusively on object-recognition robustness by encouraging text-ignoring, which is misaligned with real-world settings requiring joint object+text reasoning (e.g., autonomous driving, embodied agents).

The core benchmark design—same-scene counterfactuals crossing question type (object/text) x attack condition (clean/attacked)—is a clean and well-motivated experimental control that isolates selective text-use ability from confounds such as scene difference, which is a clear improvement over naively combining separate object-VQA and text-VQA datasets.

Substantial engineering effort in benchmark construction: hierarchical negative/attack-word sampling using the Open Images class hierarchy for object questions, LLM-generated contradictory but plausible attack phrases for open-ended text-VQA (a reportedly first attempt), and distance-controlled placement relative to key text regions and OCR boxes to avoid trivial or impossible attacks.

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation: six LVLMs of varying architectures/scales, multiple attack difficulty levels, two representative defenses (CoT, IT-RT) plus the proposed RIO-RT, detailed per-level breakdowns (Table 1), attention-map visualizations offering some mechanistic insight, LoRA placement ablation suggesting selective text use is primarily driven by the language component, and generalization experiments to external datasets (Typo-D, AI2D, ChartQA, DocVQA, InfoVQA).

Provides a novel evaluation metric (Robust-CLIP-Match) tailored to jointly capture correctness and attack-resistance in open-ended object recognition, and clearly documents reproducibility details (prompts, hyperparameters, compute cost) in the appendix.

The proposed RIO-RT defense, despite being a relatively simple SFT recipe, is shown empirically to achieve a more balanced trade-off than the ignore-text baseline (IT-RT) and inference-time CoT prompting, providing a concrete, actionable outcome from the benchmark's training split.
weaknesses: The benchmark is built entirely from a single source (TextVQA over Open Images); while the paper argues the pipeline generalizes to other dual-annotation datasets, this is not empirically demonstrated—only downstream generalization of the trained defense is tested, not benchmark construction on a second dataset, so the core claim of a broadly applicable pipeline rests partly on assertion.

Several automatic construction choices are not validated against human judgment: ground-truth object class selection uses CLIP top-1 similarity (which can be noisy or ambiguous for multi-label images), and LLM-generated (Llama-3) contradictory attack phrases for Text-Attack are not verified for quality, naturalness, or actual difficulty via human annotators, raising concerns about label noise and attack validity underlying the reported accuracy numbers.

The proposed defense (RIO-RT) is architecturally simple—balanced SFT mixture of Obj-Attack and Text-Attack samples—which, while effective, is a fairly incremental methodological contribution relative to the benchmark itself; the paper's main technical novelty is concentrated in benchmark/task design rather than the defense algorithm.

Baseline defense comparisons are somewhat narrow: only CoT prompting and a self-constructed IT-RT baseline are compared; existing published methods such as Defense-Prefix or CLIP-mirror-based approaches ([2],[39]) are not directly adapted and compared quantitatively (only discussed qualitatively as inapplicable to LVLMs), which limits the strength of claims that all existing defenses fail at this task.

The R-CLIP-M metric, while a reasonable proxy, is a similarity-based automatic metric that may not perfectly track human-perceived correctness or attack susceptibility, and no human evaluation or correlation study is provided to validate it.

Some claims of novelty (e.g., "first attempt" at open-ended text-VQA typographic attacks, "first structural foundation for training-based defenses") are somewhat strong given the relatively narrow technical departure from prior attack/defense formulations, and could be tempered.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and underexplored gap: prior typographic-attack defenses (largely CLIP zero-shot classification defenses) achieve robustness by suppressing text sensitivity entirely, which is misaligned with the joint object+text reasoning LVLMs must perform in practice.

The 'same-scene counterfactual' design principle (deriving both object- and text-centric Clean/Attack variants from the same underlying image via dual TextVQA/Open-Images annotations) is a sound methodological idea that avoids the confound of comparing across different image distributions.

The experimental scope is reasonably broad: six LVLM backbones, an inference-time defense (CoT) and two training-based defenses (IT-RT baseline and RIO-RT), attack-level ablations (hard/medium/easy; near/far), LoRA placement ablation, attention-map analysis, and cross-dataset generalization checks (Typo-D, AI2D, ChartQA, DocVQA, InfoVQA).

The paper is transparent about construction details, metrics (R-CLIP-M is a reasonable adaptation of CLIP-Match to penalize attack-word similarity), and computational cost, which aids reproducibility.
The finding that selective text use is primarily learned through the language-model component rather than the vision encoder (Table 2) is an interesting, if narrow, mechanistic observation.
weaknesses: Serious data-quality concern: in the qualitative appendix examples (Figs. 6–11), the Text-Clean/Text-Attack question is 'what kind of beer is this?' for numerous clearly unrelated images (a billboard, a wristwatch, a baseball pitcher, a whiteboard mind-map, a bottle of wine). This strongly suggests either a bug in question-image pairing during dataset construction/visualization or that the 'original TextVQA question retained' step is not correctly tied to the depicted scene, which directly undermines the core claim of faithful same-scene counterfactuals and casts doubt on the validity of the Text-VQA subset used throughout the main results.

The proposed defense (RIO-RT) is conceptually just balanced SFT on a mixture of Obj-Attack and Text-Attack data versus IT-RT's one-sided mixture; this is an expected/incremental combination rather than a novel training method, and the paper does not compare against other plausible balancing strategies, loss reweighting, or curriculum designs that might achieve similar or better trade-offs.

The benchmark is derived entirely from a single source (TextVQA/Open Images); no human verification of the automatically selected ground-truth object labels (via CLIP top-1 scoring) or of the LLM-generated text attack words is reported, raising concerns about label noise, especially since CLIP-based pseudo-labeling can be unreliable for cluttered natural scenes.

Object-centric attacks are a fairly standard word-insertion strategy already used in prior typographic-attack literature (e.g., SCAM, Cheng et al.); the main novelty is confined to the text-centric attack generation and the counterfactual pairing, which is a narrower contribution than the framing suggests.

The cross-dataset generalization study (Appendix F.2) shows mixed and sometimes contradictory results (e.g., LLaMA-3.2-11B-Vision losing text-reading on RIO-Bench's scene text but retaining it on document/chart datasets), which the paper interprets post-hoc as 'domain-specific trade-offs' without a clear explanation or additional analysis, weakening the strength of the generalization claim.

Training-based defenses are only evaluated with LoRA on modest data sizes (16k) and a single random seed/configuration per model; no variance/statistical significance is reported across runs, and no comparison to full fine-tuning or alternative PEFT methods is provided despite claiming the approach is 'architecture-agnostic.'

The evaluation metrics for open-ended object recognition (R-CLIP-M) and its top-5 CLIP similarity design are somewhat ad hoc and not validated against human judgments of correctness/robustness, leaving open whether the metric faithfully captures the intended notion of selective text use.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and important gap in prior work: typographic-attack robustness research has implicitly assumed text should be ignored, whereas real-world LVLM deployment requires selective text use. This reframing is well-motivated and clearly articulated.

The core methodological contribution—constructing same-scene counterfactuals by exploiting dual annotations (TextVQA + Open Images) to jointly probe object- and text-centric questions under clean/attacked conditions—is a clever and non-trivial engineering solution that meaningfully improves on naively combining separate object-VQA and text-VQA datasets.

Experimental coverage is extensive: six LVLMs spanning different architectures/scales, multiple attack difficulty levels (hard/medium/easy for objects; near/mid/far for text), ablations on LoRA parameter placement, attention-map visualizations, and a generalization study to external benchmarks (Typo-D, AI2D, ChartQA, DocVQA, InfoVQA).

The proposed RIO-RT defense is simple (standard SFT with balanced attack exposure) yet demonstrates a clear, consistent qualitative difference from the ignore-text baseline (IT-RT): it preserves or improves text-reading accuracy while still gaining object robustness, supporting the paper's central claim that selective text use is a learnable, distinct capability.

The finding that selective text-use ability is primarily governed by the language model rather than the vision encoder is an interesting mechanistic insight that meaningfully differentiates this work from prior vision-centric defenses.

Reproducibility is well supported: appendix provides detailed dataset statistics, attack rendering/placement algorithms, LLM prompts, evaluation metric definitions (R-CLIP-M), and compute cost breakdowns.
weaknesses: The benchmark is built entirely on a single source (TextVQA/Open Images natural scene images); although a generalization study to other datasets is included, the core training/eval subsets share the same visual domain and OCR/annotation style, which may limit diversity of real-world scenarios (e.g., no embodied/driving imagery despite these being motivating examples in the intro).

Typographic attacks are simple rendered text overlays with randomized font/color/position rather than photorealistic, scene-consistent insertions (e.g., as in SceneTAP); this is acknowledged as a design choice but reduces realism relative to some prior work and may make the task somewhat easier or differently distributed than physical-world attacks.

The R-CLIP-M metric for object OE evaluation is relatively complex and its reliability (e.g., sensitivity to CLIP's own biases, top-5 thresholding choices) is not stress-tested; likewise, ground-truth class selection via CLIP top-1 similarity could introduce label noise that isn't quantified via human validation.

No human study or manual quality check is reported for the automatically generated attack words (LLM-generated contradictory phrases) or the MC negative sampling, so the difficulty/naturalness of some "hard" attacks (or occasional ambiguous cases) is not independently verified.

Defense baselines are somewhat limited (CoT and a single reconstructed IT-RT baseline); other existing typographic defenses cited in related work (e.g., projection-based, mirror-reflection-based) are not empirically compared even in adapted form, aside from the argument that they don't directly transfer to LVLMs.

Training data size for RIO-RT is modest (16k samples) and while a data-scaling ablation is provided, all experiments use LoRA fine-tuning only; it's unclear how findings would hold under full fine-tuning or larger-scale training, which could affect generalizability of the conclusions about language-model-driven selective text use.

strengths: Novel and practically motivated task formulation (RIO-VQA) that identifies a genuine blind spot in existing typographic-attack robustness evaluation: current object-centric protocols cannot distinguish 'true robustness' from indiscriminate text-suppression.

The same-scene counterfactual design (fixing the scene, varying only question intent and text condition) is a clean and effective methodological choice that meaningfully reduces confounds compared to naively combining separate object-VQA and text-VQA datasets.

Thorough and carefully engineered benchmark construction: hierarchical negative sampling for MC options, LLM-generated contradiction-based attacks for text-VQA, two complementary attack realism levels (controlled overlay and SceneTAP-based scene-coherent insertion with OCR-region safeguards), and a new R-CLIP-M metric that explicitly penalizes attack-word-induced bias in open-ended predictions.

Solid empirical validation of dataset quality via human audits with reasonable inter-annotator agreement (Gwet's AC1 0.89-0.94), which supports the claim that observed failures reflect genuine model behavior rather than dataset artifacts.

Broad and modern experimental coverage: 6 LVLM architectures/scales plus additional evaluation on newer open-source families (Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5) and closed-source frontier models (GPT-5.4, Gemini-2.5-Pro), along with multiple defense baselines (CoT, IT-RT, RIO-RT).

Insightful supporting analyses beyond the main benchmark results: attack-difficulty-level ablations, LoRA parameter-placement ablation (showing language-side adaptation matters most), attention-map visualizations that provide a plausible mechanistic explanation of the read/ignore behavior, and generalization checks to Typo-D and external text-VQA benchmarks.

The central finding (object-centric defenses gain robustness at the cost of text-reading, while balanced training mitigates this) is clearly demonstrated and has real significance for how the field should evaluate and design typographic-attack defenses.
weaknesses: The benchmark is derived entirely from a single source dataset (TextVQA/Open Images); scene diversity, image domains, and text types are therefore constrained, and it remains unclear how well findings transfer to substantially different real-world settings mentioned as motivation (e.g., traffic signs, embodied-agent instructions) beyond the limited external generalization experiments provided.

RIO-RT, the proposed defense, is essentially a straightforward SFT baseline on a balanced attack mixture; the algorithmic novelty is modest, and the paper explicitly frames it as a minimal reference rather than a fully developed defense, which is reasonable but limits the technical contribution beyond the benchmark itself.

Some quantitative results are only partially explained: e.g., the divergence between RIO-Bench text-degradation and preserved external text-VQA performance for LLaMA-3.2-11B-Vision under IT-RT is interesting but only briefly discussed, leaving open questions about the generality of the 'domain-specific trade-off' claim.

The comparison against prior defenses is limited to a single LVLM-focused method (CoT) plus the paper's own two baselines, since most prior CLIP-centric defenses are not directly applicable; while this is justified, it somewhat narrows the empirical contrast against the broader defense literature.

The human audit, while showing strong agreement, is based on a relatively small sample (400 out of tens of thousands of instances), which may not fully capture rarer failure modes such as edge cases in attack-word plausibility or occasional over-strong/unanswerable text attacks.

The R-CLIP-M metric and CLIP-based ground-truth label selection introduce dependence on CLIP's own biases and similarity judgments, which could subtly affect both benchmark construction (label selection, negative sampling) and evaluation in ways not fully explored.

strengths: Identifies and formalizes a genuinely important and underexplored gap: existing typographic-attack robustness evaluations are object-centric and cannot distinguish 'true robustness' from simply suppressing all textual cues, which is problematic for real-world settings requiring both object recognition and scene-text reading (e.g., autonomous driving, embodied AI).

The same-scene counterfactual benchmark design is a strong methodological contribution: by holding the underlying scene fixed and varying only question intent (object vs. text) and text condition (clean vs. attack), RIO-Bench substantially reduces confounds (e.g., text density/layout priors) that would otherwise contaminate cross-dataset comparisons.

Clever reuse of dual annotations in TextVQA/Open Images to construct paired object- and text-centric questions on identical images, with a well-thought-out hierarchical negative-sampling scheme for MC options and a spatial/semantic difficulty-level design for attacks.

Introduces a new metric (R-CLIP-M) that explicitly penalizes attack-word retrieval bias in open-ended object recognition, addressing a real blind spot of the standard CLIP-M metric under typographic attacks.

Comprehensive empirical study: six LVLM architectures/scales for main experiments, plus an additional scaling study across open-source model families (Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5) and closed-source frontier models (GPT-5.4, Gemini-2.5-Pro), revealing that scaling and closed-source strength do not resolve the read-or-ignore trade-off.

The benchmark quality is validated via a human audit with high inter-annotator agreement (Gwet's AC1 0.89-0.94), supporting the claim that observed model failures reflect real behavior rather than dataset artifacts.

Rich supporting analyses (attack-level sensitivity, LoRA parameter-placement ablation, attention-map visualization, out-of-benchmark generalization to Typo-D/AI2D/ChartQA/DocVQA/InfoVQA, training-data-size ablation) that meaningfully deepen the empirical story rather than being superficial add-ons.

The proposed RIO-RT baseline, while intentionally simple, provides a clear proof-of-concept that balanced exposure to both object- and text-centric attacked instances can mitigate the read/ignore trade-off, and the paper is appropriately modest about its scope (explicitly framed as a reference baseline, not a final solution).
Strong reproducibility: detailed appendix on data construction, prompts, attack generation, evaluation metrics, and compute costs.
weaknesses: The benchmark is built entirely on a single source dataset (TextVQA/Open Images); while extensible in principle, the actual released benchmark may inherit biases/scene distribution limitations of this specific source, and generalization to other scene-text domains (e.g., documents, dense multilingual signage) is only partially explored in the appendix.

The main proposed defense (RIO-RT) is a straightforward SFT on a balanced attack mixture; the algorithmic novelty is modest, which is acceptable given the benchmark/dataset framing, but the paper could more clearly state upfront that this is the intended contribution type to set expectations.

Some generalization results are only partially explained: e.g., IT-RT severely degrades text-reading on RIO-Bench for LLaMA-3.2-11B-Vision but preserves it on external text-VQA benchmarks (Sec. F.2), suggesting the observed trade-off may be partly domain/benchmark-specific rather than a fully general property of 'ignore-text' defenses; more discussion of why this discrepancy occurs would strengthen the claims.

The SceneTAP-Attack pipeline is modified from the original (adding OCR-masking safeguards and different placement constraints), which is well-justified but makes direct quantitative comparison to the original SceneTAP paper's numbers not straightforward.

Distractor-text generation for text-centric attacks relies on an LLM (Llama-3) prompted to produce contradicting short phrases; despite the human audit showing high validity, the diversity and adversarial strength of these generated distractors is not deeply characterized (e.g., no analysis of failure/rejection rate of LLM-generated attacks).

Training-based defenses (IT-RT, RIO-RT) are trained only on Overlay-Attack data and evaluated for transfer to SceneTAP/other benchmarks, but the training split does not include scene-coherent generative insertions at all, so the demonstrated transfer, while encouraging, is based on a fairly narrow training distribution relative to the full space of realistic typographic attacks the paper motivates.
